← Stair lift bid calculator

How much to charge to install a stair lift

Accessibility contractors get shopped on a published $3,995 stair lift installed Facebook special. Those numbers cannot see the rail or the chair. A straight indoor rail with a standard seated chair on wood treads is a different job from a curved custom-bent rail with a heavy-duty power-swivel chair, open-riser attach, a folding rail, and a dedicated circuit.

Open the free stair lift bid calculator

Price the rail and the chair, not the $3,995 dump

A stair lift is a rail, then a chair, then an attach. A straight one-flight rail is a kit. A mid-landing is a second piece. Outdoor is weatherized. Curved is a template and a custom bend. Matching an installed special on a curved-plus-circuit job is how a sold aging-in-place install becomes a loss when the custom rail and the electrician eat the margin.

Standard versus power swivel on the same stair

Homeowners usually start from the standard seated special, then ask whether a power swivel or a heavy-duty chair is “a little more.” On the same rail and the same attach it is not a little more. A power swivel is a motor and extra set time. Heavy-duty is weight rating and a heavier chassis. The calculator prices all five chairs on the stair you already counted so you can quote the upgrade instead of matching the standard number on a heavy-duty job.

A straight rail is not a curved rail

The cheap special is almost always a straight indoor rail, a standard chair, wood treads, no fold, no electrician. A curved heavy-duty open-riser job is a different crew day. Matching a published installed number on that job is how a sold aging-in-place install becomes a loss.

This is not a wheelchair ramp, a walk-in tub, or a home elevator

A wheelchair ramp is carpentry — rise-to-run, landings, slope — a platform, not a chair on a rail. A walk-in tub is bathroom plumbing and an alcove. A walk-in shower is tile, slope, and glass. A home elevator is a shaft. This prices a stair lift: the rail, the chair, the attach, and the extras.

Customer-supplied lifts are not a free set

Owners also shop a second special: “I already bought one on Facebook — just install it for $795.” Zeroing the rail and chair invoices drops the bid. The set hours stay. A rail that is too short or missing brackets is a second trip. See should I install a customer-supplied stair lift for the three-way comparison on the same stair.

Hospital discharge is not the weekday bid

Families also shop a third special: “Mom comes home Friday — same $3,995 on Saturday?” A stair-lift rail ships from the factory. Next-day air is a starting expedite on top of the rail invoice. Working around someone who just came home is a slower set. Saturday is time-and-a-half plus a second dispatch. See should I expedite a stair lift for hospital discharge for weekday versus discharge week versus Saturday on the same stair.

Walk-away price

Load the wage with payroll burden. Add overhead as a share of direct cost. Then take margin as a share of the customer’s price, not a markup on cost. The walk-away number is total cost. A proposed price under that number loses money before you take anything out of it.

This page is a walkthrough of the arithmetic in the stair lift bid calculator. It is not a building-code determination, an accessibility approval, a medical-device prescription, or a price you should copy onto a contract.

Common questions

How much should I charge to install a stair lift?

Charge from lift count, rail, chair, attach, and extras — not a published $3,995 installed special. A straight indoor rail with a standard seated chair on wood treads is a different job from a curved custom-bent rail with a heavy-duty power-swivel chair, open-riser attach, a folding rail, and a dedicated circuit.

Is a straight rail the same bid as a curved rail?

No. A straight one-flight rail is a kit. A mid-landing is a second piece. Outdoor is weatherized. Curved is a template and a custom bend. Matching an installed special on a curved-plus-circuit job is how a sold aging-in-place install becomes a loss when the custom rail and the electrician eat the margin.

How do the chair, the attach, and extras change a stair lift price?

A standard seated chair is the cheap-special unit. Perch is cheaper. Power swivel is the last-minute upgrade. Power-pack adds a powered footrest. Heavy-duty is weight rating. Wood treads are the cheap attach. Concrete needs masonry bits. Open-riser needs more hardware. Folding rail, extra charge point, dedicated circuit, existing-lift removal, permit, and weather kit do not live in a published installed dump.

Is this the same as a wheelchair ramp, a walk-in tub, or a home elevator?

No. A wheelchair ramp is carpentry — rise-to-run, landings, slope — a platform, not a chair on a rail. A walk-in tub is bathroom plumbing and an alcove. A walk-in shower is tile, slope, and glass. A home elevator is a shaft. This prices a stair lift: the rail, the chair, the attach, and the extras.

should-i-expedite-a-stair-lift-for-hospi.text:
← Stair lift bid calculator

Should I expedite a stair lift for hospital discharge?

Families call with a weekday number: “Mom comes home Friday. Can you put it in Saturday? Same $3,995?” That sounds like the same stair. It is not the same freight ticket and it is not the same crew day. A stair-lift rail ships from the factory. Next-day air is a starting expedite on top of the rail invoice. Working around someone who just came home is the same wage on a slower set. Saturday is time-and-a-half plus a second dispatch, because a Friday discharge is not a stop you combine with a weekday route.

Open the free stair lift bid calculator

Discharge week is not the weekday bid

A weekday slot still carries the wage and the ground freight already in the rail invoice. Discharge week adds a starting next-day rail ticket and clock hours on the rail, the set, the chair, the attach, and the punch-list. On a typical cheap special — $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, eight miles — the weekday bid is $5,333.37. Discharge week is $6,190.67. After-hours Saturday is $6,692.99. The walk-away jumps from $4,266.69 to $5,354.39. Taking $4,500 to “just do Saturday at the weekday number” covers the weekday slot and loses $854.39 after hours.

The rush special is more tempting when the stair is already a custom bend and they want it before discharge. The weekday bid is $20,983.85. Discharge week is $22,046.79. After-hours is $23,222.14 and the walk-away is $18,577.71. Taking $2,495 to “just hang something this weekend” still loses money — even on the weekday.

This is not a customer-supplied lift or a walk-in tub

Customer-supplied lifts are their Facebook unit and an install-only number — see should I install a customer-supplied stair lift. Discharge week is when the rail can arrive and who is in the house. A walk-in tub Saturday is alcove plumbing overtime. A toilet Saturday is an overflowing bowl. This prices a stair lift: the rail, the expedite ticket, and the extras.

How to use the comparison

Open the stair lift bid calculator, pick the cheap-special or losing-job preset, and put their Saturday number in “price you’re considering.” The access table scores that number against a weekday slot, discharge week while they stay home, and Saturday / after-hours. Nothing is uploaded.

This is the same arithmetic as how much to charge to install a stair lift. It is not a medical-discharge plan, a labor-law determination, or a reason to refuse a customer — it is the walk-away number on each access window.

Common questions

Should I expedite a stair lift for hospital discharge?

Only after you price next-day rail freight plus a slower occupied set, or Saturday overtime plus a second dispatch. A $3,995 Facebook special on a straight indoor rail sits under that walk-away number even on a weekday slot.

Does a discharge-week install change the bid?

Yes. Same wage, slower rail, set, chair, and punch-list, plus a starting next-day rail ticket. On a typical straight indoor rail the discharge-week bid is $6,190.67 versus $5,333.37 when they can wait for a weekday slot and ground freight.

Can I take the weekday $4,500 number on Saturday?

Usually not on the job they actually want. On a cheap straight indoor rail the after-hours walk-away is $5,354.39. $4,500 covers a weekday slot and loses $854.39 after hours. On a curved heavy-duty job, $2,495 still loses money even on the weekday.

Should I install a customer-supplied stair lift?

Owners call with a used unit in the garage: “I already bought one on Facebook. Can you just install it for $795?” That sounds like free margin because the rail and chair invoices left the bid. They did not leave the trip, the template, the set hours, or the chance that the rail is an indoor kit on an outdoor stair.

Open the free stair lift bid calculator

Zeroing the lift is not a free install

A contractor-supplied straight indoor rail still carries the rail and chair invoices. An owner-supplied unit that actually fits zeros those lines and keeps the same set hours. On a typical cheap special — $42 wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, 20% target margin, eight miles — the contractor-supplied bid is about $5,333. Zeroing a $2,200 rail and a $650 chair drops it to about $1,236, but the owner-supplied walk-away stays about $989. Taking the Facebook special to “just install what they bought” at $795 still loses about $194.

Common questions

Should I install a stair lift the customer bought on Facebook?

Only after you price the set without the rail and chair invoices. Templating their used rail is still a trip and crew hours. A $795 install-only special often sits under that walk-away number even when the lift is free to you.

Does a customer-supplied stair lift make the $795 installed special profitable?

Usually not. Zeroing a $2,200 rail and a $650 chair drops the bid, but loaded labor, attach hardware, travel, and overhead stay. On a typical straight indoor rail the owner-supplied walk-away is still above $795. A rail that is too short or missing brackets adds a second trip.

What if the used lift does not fit the stair?

That is a second dispatch plus missing brackets or a charge point they did not have. Price that callback on the same stair before you agree to install whatever they rolled into the driveway. The calculator adds a starting inspect trip and missing-hardware kit on top of your current rates.

vs-a-flat-rate-stair-lift-special.html.text:
← Stair Lift Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat "$3,995 installed" stair lift special

"$3,995 installed" is not a price for a stair lift — it is a price for one specific rail, one chair, and one tread attach, quietly applied to every staircase the template goes up.

What a flat "$3,995 installed" special is

A flat installed rate is the fastest way to quote: one headline number on a postcard or a website, next to a photo of a straight staircase. Homeowners shop it because it is easy to compare between bids, and it is the number an owner holding a competitor's flyer — or a family arranging a hospital discharge on a deadline — will ask you to match on their own stairs.

The number behind it was set for one job — usually the cheapest configuration (a straight one-flight rail, a standard seated chair, wood treads, no fold, no circuit, no removal) — and then reused for every lift afterward, whether or not the next staircase looks anything like the one the rate was set on.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter the lift count, travel, plus rail (straight, landing, outdoor, or curved), chair (perch, standard, power swivel, power pack, or heavy-duty), and tread attach (wood, concrete, or open-riser), along with extras such as a folding rail, an extra charge point, a dedicated circuit, removing an existing lift, a permit, and a weatherizing kit. It prices the rail, the chair, the attach, and the extras separately, and returns a walk-away price and extra-work share below which the job loses money — for this staircase, not a generic one.

Job$3,995 specialWalk-away priceVerdict
Cheap special: 1 straight rail, standard chair, wood treads$3,995.00$4,266.69Short $271.69
Typical aging-in-place: 1 straight rail, power swivel, wood, folding rail, circuit, permit$3,995.00$6,846.45Short $2,851.45
Losing job: 1 curved rail, heavy-duty chair, open-riser, fold, circuit, pull existing lift$3,995.00$16,643.33Short $12,648.33

Worked using this calculator's own starting kits at a $42 crew wage, 30% payroll burden, 15% overhead on direct cost, and a 20% target margin — the form's own defaults, not a number invented for this page. Open the calculator's presets to check any row yourself.

What a flat installed special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same installed rate whether the job is a straight one-flight rail with a standard chair on wood treads or a curved custom-bent rail with a heavy-duty power-swivel chair on an open-riser stair — several times the labor and material for the same "one stair lift." Prices the rail from the entered rail type, chair, and tread attach, so the two jobs above come out at different numbers instead of one.
Prices "a stair lift" as one rail-and-chair set, with no separate line for templating and bending a curved rail, a heavy-duty or power chassis, open-riser hardware, a folding rail at the landing, a dedicated circuit, or pulling and hauling the old lift. Times the rail bend, the chair grade, the attach hardware, the fold, the circuit, and the removal as their own extra-work hours, so that work shows up instead of being absorbed into the flat rate or skipped.
Assumes a straight rail, a standard chair, wood treads, and no fold, circuit, removal, or weatherizing, so a curved rail, a power chair, open-riser hardware, or a dedicated circuit gets quoted the same as a job that needs none of that. Adds fold, extra charge point, circuit, removal, permit, and weatherizing hours and material only for what was entered, so the two jobs price differently.
Bakes payroll burden into a round "installed rate" nobody re-derives, so the rate quietly drifts from the crew's real loaded cost. Loads the entered hourly wage by the entered payroll-burden percentage every time, so labor cost tracks the actual burden rather than a memorized rate.
Gives the installer a price to quote, not a number to check a quote against when a family asks to match a cheaper straight-rail special on a curved, powered, open-riser job — often on a hospital-discharge deadline. Reports the walk-away price and the extra-work share of the job, so a shopped price can be scored against real cost before the installer commits to it.

A flat installed special is not wrong because it is simple — it is wrong when it is applied outside the one job it was built for, and nothing about a postcard rate tells you when that has happened. This calculator does not replace judgment about your market; it replaces the arithmetic a flat rate skips.

Common questions

Why does a flat "$3,995 installed" stair lift special get the price wrong?

Because the labor and material scale with the rail, the chair, the tread attach, and the extras, not with "a stair lift" alone. A straight one-flight rail with a standard seated chair on wood treads is a different job from a curved custom-bent rail with a heavy-duty power-swivel chair on an open-riser stair, a folding rail for the door, a dedicated circuit, and pulling the old lift. A flat installed rate quotes both the same and is wrong on one of them every time.

What does a flat installed rate usually leave out entirely?

The bend, the swivel, the fold, and the electrician. A published installed price is set on the cheapest configuration it was ever quoted against — a straight rail, a standard chair, wood treads, no fold, no circuit, no removal — and has nowhere to put the hours for a custom-bent curved rail, a power-swivel or heavy-duty chair, open-riser hardware, a folding rail at the bottom landing, a dedicated circuit run, or pulling and hauling the old lift. A contractor pricing off the flat rate alone is short before the template goes up the stairs.

How much do the rail, chair, attach, and extras actually add over the flat rate?

On this calculator's own worked examples, at a $42 crew wage, 30% burden, 15% overhead, and a 20% target margin: a straight one-flight rail, a standard chair, and wood treads walks away at $4,266.69, already $271.69 over its own $3,995.00 special. The typical aging-in-place job — the same straight rail with a power-swivel chair, a folding rail, a dedicated circuit, and a permit — walks away at $6,846.45, $2,851.45 short of the same $3,995.00. A curved custom-bent rail with a heavy-duty chair, open-riser attach, the fold, the circuit, and pulling the existing lift walks away at $16,643.33 — $12,648.33 short, more than four times the flat rate on the same one-lift job. The rail, the chair, the attach, and the extras move the number far more than "one stair lift" alone.

Is a flat installed rate ever the right way to quote a stair lift?

For something close to the one job it was actually priced on — a straight one-flight rail, a standard seated chair, wood treads, no fold, no circuit, no removal — a flat rate can land close, and on this calculator's own numbers the cheap-special job comes out only a few hundred dollars over it. The risk is applying the same number to a curved rail, a power or heavy-duty chair, an open-riser stair, a folding rail, a dedicated circuit, or pulling an old lift without noticing, because the flat rate does not know which job it is looking at and neither does the installer until the rail is templated.

Does this calculator know what to charge in my market?

No. It has no data on local rates or what competitors charge. It takes the rail, the chair, the tread attach, and the extras, plus your loaded labor and overhead, and turns them into a walk-away price and extra-work share for the job you describe — the arithmetic a flat rate skips, not a market survey.

Nothing here says or implies that quoting a flat "$3,995 installed" special is a bad-faith practice — it is a common, honest shortcut that works until the job stops matching the one the rate was set on. This page describes where that shortcut breaks down, not a fault in anyone who uses it.

← Stair Lift Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. AutoVu Solutions

Two different shapes: AutoVu Solutions is CRM and field-service management software for running a stairlift dealership's quoting, scheduling, and parts-and-service accounts across a whole book of jobs. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one stair cost, given its rail, chair, attach, and extras, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

AutoVu Solutions sells CRM and field-service management software built specifically for the stairlift and wider lift trade. Its publicly described feature set covers custom quote templates by lift type with pre-defined pricing structures, an appointments diary for booking sales and service engineers, and an accounts module that invoices stairlift sales and parts linked to an installation or service job, then nets supplier cost invoices against sales invoices for profit-and-loss tracking across the business. It is offered with a free tier for a small team and paid tiers as usage grows, sold as an ongoing account for a dealership rather than a single-job tool. Common questions

Should I use this calculator or AutoVu Solutions?

They do different jobs, and an accessibility dealer of any size may end up using both. AutoVu Solutions sells CRM and field-service management software built for the stairlift and lift trade: custom quote templates by lift type with pre-set pricing, an appointments diary for sales and service engineers, and an accounts module that invoices lift sales and parts against installation and service jobs and nets supplier cost against sales invoices for profit-and-loss tracking, run as an ongoing account for the whole dealership. This calculator does one narrower thing: starting from lift count, straight versus landing versus outdoor versus curved rail, perch versus standard versus power-swivel versus power-pack versus heavy-duty chair, wood versus concrete versus open-riser attach, folding rail, an extra charge point, a dedicated circuit, removing an existing lift, a permit trip, and a weather kit, it turns that into the per-job price and the walk-away price below which the job loses money. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type. A dealership already running quoting, dispatch, and job-and-parts accounting across a full install schedule is better served by AutoVu Solutions or a comparable platform; an installer who wants an instant, private gut-check on what one stair should cost before opening a business system is in the right place here.

Does this calculator handle a customer-supplied lift?

Yes, and it is where a flat "installed" special breaks. A lift someone already bought secondhand is not the same job as one sold and installed together: no equipment margin, and the fit, wiring, and rail condition still have to be checked before a crew commits labor to it. This calculator's own how-to-charge article covers the contractor-supplied-versus-customer-supplied split in more depth; the calculator itself prices the labor and extras either way, and the walk-away price still tells you the floor.
